text.p: Israeli shares continued to rise on Thursday in the second day of trading after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was vindicated of a corruption scandal, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares rose 0.58 percent, or 1.46 points, to 252.10 on an all-share turnover of 91 million shekels against 83 million shekels on Wednesday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 0.33 percent higher at 262.36.

"This is the second day of trading (since Netanyahu's vindication). In the last two days people have felt happier without the burden of the Bar-On affair. The issue will remain with us for a long time, but the direct impact on the market has vanished. The market is coming back up to its upper trend," said Eli Nahum, head of trading at Zannex Securities.
Prosecutors on Sunday rejected a police recommendation that they should charge Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust in the short-lived appointment in January of Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.

"This is not the normal picture during holidays. We have had a good two days of trading," Nahum said. "The market is waiting for the announcement of the interest rates, but the macro-economic environment is enough to justify the continuing of a positive trend in the market."
Trading hours on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange were reduced on Thursday for the intermediate days of Passover.
The Bank of Israel announced on Thursday after the trading day that it was leaving unchanged at 13.9 percent its key lending rate for May.
"People were waiting to see what interest rates will be but the market doesn't expect a cut," said Doron Zur at Sahar Securities.

The most traded stock stock on Thursday was Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which rose 1.75 percent to 17,172 agorot on volume of 17.3 million shekels. Nahum said the stock was now rebounding after losses of about 25 percent in the last month. "We believe Teva is a very good buying opportunity," he said.

Super-Sol rose 3.50 percent to 1,012 agorot after Morgan Stanley announced on Wednesday it had increased its holding to 7.88 percent and had become a major shareholder. Under Israeli regulations investors become major shareholders when their holdings exceed five percent.

El-Rov rose the maximum 10 percent to 2,878 agorot after a group of funds owned by U.S. investor Goerge Soros announced on Wednesday it had bought an additional 7.12 percent in the company raising its stake to 23.12 percent.

Other active shares included Israel Discount Bank, which rose 0.75 percent to 347 agorot on volume of 5.5 million shekels; and Bank Leumi which closed unchanged at 565 agorot on volume of 3.6 million shekels.
